title: History and lineage
thesis: Many of the conventions that now define roguelikes (permadeath, random levels, the character grid, the lone thief who uses magic items) began as technical constraints, borrowings from tabletop play and fiction, or accidents of distribution, not as design doctrine. The genre spread because Rogue's code was closed and later games' code was open, so it grew through recreation, forking and community stewardship. Knowing that lineage lets a designer tell which conventions still earn their place, and shows why the genre's history has to be actively recovered and kept playable.

sections.heading: Before the computer: wargames, pulp fantasy and generative toys
sections.brief: Argue that the roguelike's DNA predates computers. Start with Michael Brough's two roots of D&D (Chainmail and historical wargames on one side, early fantasy fiction on the other) and his case that the device-using thief descends from Leiber's Gray Mouser via D&D's rogue; set this beside Noah Swartz's evidence that Michael Toy was probably influenced by Le Guin's The Tombs of Atuan, especially the amulet quest. Bring in Craddock on early creators wanting a computerised D&D that offloads dice-rolling, Brough on pulp short stories shaping episodic session structure, and the naming question: Glenn Wichman says Rogue was picked because it was short to type, while Darren Grey argues the word's connotations still shaped the design. Then widen out to pre-digital generators and borrowing: Gygax's random-dungeon dice tables (which John Harris says produced meaningless layouts, as some roguelikes do), Pichlmair's Mahjong lineage and paper word-wheel, Ulam's solitaire-driven Monte Carlo method, and Toussaint's rhythms. End with Brough's open question about reading older sources with uncomfortable attitudes, and the practical guidance: read and play your genre's ancestors, because the conventions you inherit came from somewhere specific.

sections.heading: Proto-roguelikes: the games Rogue did not name
sections.brief: Argue that many people arrived at roguelike ideas at the same time, and that circumstance (distribution, preservation, institutional tolerance of games) decided which one gave the genre its name. Open with Craddock: Beneath Apple Manor had the ideas but did not spread over networks the way Rogue did. Then Aaron Reed's contrast between deterministic equation-solving games (Hammurabi, Lunar Lander) and Mike Mayfield's randomly generated Star Trek, which he says has much in common with what Rogue would name. Give Dan Norder's Chase its own thread: Dartmouth BASIC and Kemeny's tolerance of games, the rules added variant by variant (teleport, wait, last stand), experimental rule variants, its unknown author, and its descendants Robotron and Robots for UNIX. Then Duke Dougal's Wilderness (1979), which already had spells, scrolls, levelling and a Wumpus-like underworld. Close with Reed's point that genres calcified around 1985-87 for business reasons, and the guidance: the pre-genre experiments are a cheap source of untried rules, so play them in emulators.

sections.heading: Why Rogue: surprise, scarcity and conventions that began as constraints
sections.brief: This is the chapter's design core. Lead with Michael Toy's motive: authored adventures cannot surprise their own author, so he wanted a game that kept its wonder even for him. Then show that much of what became canon was constraint: Aaron Reed says early procgen was a necessity because hand-made worlds did not fit in memory, and the Rise of the Roguelite panel says permadeath and level randomness came largely from technical limits, yet modern games feel obliged to justify them in-world. Set Eiríkr Åsheim's permacomputing reading against this: Rogue's frugality (procgen to minimise assets, playable over a phone line, small team, portable for 40 years) is a virtue worth keeping, not just an accident. Use the concrete artefacts as examples: the number 26, Rogue's generation loop placing monsters and items room by room (Mark Gritter), the scare-monster scroll, monster counts growing letter by letter across Rogue, Hack and NetHack (George Moromisato), the slime mold joke, high-score tables as early metaprogression, and door transitions that outlived loading screens (John Bond). End with guidance: for each inherited convention, ask whether it still serves your game or only survives as habit, and if you keep it, keep it for a reason rather than an in-fiction excuse.

sections.heading: The terminal and the character grid
sections.brief: Argue that the roguelike's look is a hardware artefact with a long history, which designers now keep by choice. Lead with Tabitha Sable on curses: Ken Arnold lifted vi's redraw code into a library and Rogue became its killer app; then Nick Montfort's point that Rogue needed cursor-addressable terminals (you could play Adventure on a teletype but not Rogue). Converge Sable's termcap/terminfo and teletype-legacy material with the Roguelike Celebration 2020 preview summary of the same story; then Montfort on how the monospace grid came from the typewriter and the 80 columns from the punch card, with Pichlmair's Senet as the far end of grid movement. Close with what came after: ncurses, ANSI and BBS art (JP LeBreton), ZZT as an early seed of mods, terminal Tetris, and the Adams brothers' half-joking 16-colour ASCII limit for Dwarf Fortress as a deliberate constraint. Guidance: if you choose ASCII or a grid, know what it buys (portability, abstraction, low asset cost) rather than adopting it as nostalgia.

sections.heading: Closed source, many children: the Hack, Moria and Rogue lines
sections.brief: Argue that the genre multiplied because Rogue's source was withheld: Dan Stormont and Michael Howk and Santiago Zapata independently say people had to recreate Rogue from memory, and Craddock shows Jay Fenlason writing Hack after a glimpse of Rogue on a school trip. This convergence is the section's spine. Then trace the lines: Hack's spread on Usenix tapes into Brouwer's Hack and NetHack (and how Fenlason's original differs), Zapata's framing of Hack as world interaction (the game as Dungeon Master) versus Moria as more content and setting, Moria's tape distribution, its abandoned real-time version and its influence on Toy and on Caves of Qud, Angband as 'Moria but more', and John Harris's forgotten Rogue line (Advanced Rogue to XRogue). Include the 1993 Usenet debate that coined 'roguelike' as the least unpopular name, then side branches: Larn and Omega's towns and gods, ADOM's origins and 1998 peak, Alphaman as an isolated sci-fi branch, and features that came from the lineage and its servers: bones files inspiring Dwarf Fortress's Legends, NetHack's 1999 conduct tracking before console achievements, shared bones and mail on shell servers, and MAngband's real-time multiplayer. End with the lesson: two design directions (deeper world interaction versus more content) recur throughout the genre, and the 'Rogue but more' pattern is how most of it grew.

sections.heading: Forks, variants and stewardship of open games
sections.brief: Where the previous section is about closed code forcing recreation, this one is about open code and what it does to a game over decades. Lead with Craddock's contrast: Hack's permissive notice led to NetHack's DevTeam keeping the game 'under lock and key', while Angband split into player-maintained variants that some players never leave; then Kes on NetHack variants cross-pollinating into untraceable version trees, and Evan Debenham on hundreds of Pixel Dungeon variants keeping the game alive after its last update (with Shattered and Sil-Q as variants that rebalance rather than add). Then stewardship: Izchak Miller as NetHack's non-programming 'librarian', Nick McConnell on Angband players each holding a different version as 'the' game, the code and learndb of NetHack and Crawl accumulating their history and odd ideas, robotfindskitten as a folk game with 50 ports, and the open-source randomizer scene. Set the community-ownership story against Kaysa Konopljak's counter-case: DotA's thousand authors reduced to four, the Ms. Pac-Man creators pulling up the ladder, and forum deletion erasing the record of community design. End with guidance for maintainers: choose a licence and governance model deliberately, because they decide whether your game becomes a single curated canon or a living family of variants, and who gets credit.

sections.heading: Into the mainstream: Diablo, Mystery Dungeon, card roguelikes and the renaissance
sections.brief: Trace how the genre's ideas reached commercial games and then took them over. Lead with the convergent Diablo evidence: the NetHack DevTeam heard Blizzard North pitched it as NetHack with graphics and sound, David Brevik says Rogue, Moria and Angband turned his party RPG into a roguelike, and the trivia answer credits Moria. Then Chunsoft's Mystery Dungeon series as the long-running commercial classical line (John Harris). Give card roguelikes their own lineage: Benjamin Berman on Magic's tournament permadeath, the 'nothing is original' tech tree, Card Hunter and Dream Quest bringing permadeath back, and Gavin Verhey's Shandalar. Then Andrew Doull's arc from lone 'fantasy heartbreakers' through the 7DRL-sparked renaissance to Spelunky and Slay the Spire, set against Scott Burger's Steam data showing growth since 2019 with no single traditional-roguelike leader. Finish with origin stories of modern games (Slay the Spire, Caves of Qud, HyperRogue, Noita and the falling-sand line, Brogue's enchant scroll replacing XP) and the guidance that genre ideas travel best when lifted into a new form, not copied whole.

sections.heading: Keeping games alive: recovery, restoration and provenance
sections.brief: Argue that roguelike history is fragile and that preservation means keeping games playable and their human stories recorded. Open with the two principles that converge: John Harris says a game is only lost when nobody plays it, and Kes says small human stories in development history will fade unless kept; add Zack Johnson's point that random generation resists documentation, so generative games especially need preserving in playable form. Then the recovery stories as worked cases: the lost Usenix tapes and the confusion they caused, Brian Harvey still holding Hack's 1982 source, Duke Dougal buying and repairing a Sorcerer to recover Wilderness and retyping a magazine printout, Alphaman's source released via a fan, Diablo reverse-engineered from a leaked symbol table, the broken post-5.3 Rogue source and the Roguelike Restoration Project. Present Michael Howk's restoration technique in detail (comment out rather than delete, note every modern change, hunt PDP-11 assumptions, keep the authors' banter). Then provenance and memory: Kes's asphynx hunt and its dead emails, version control as story, Crawl's learndb, RogueBasin and the move off Usenet, hint lines dying into wikis, MADE's exhibits, and Cara Esten Hurtle on queer and adult games that retro communities leave out. End with practical guidance for developers about their own work: keep source and history public, licence it, and document generators and decisions so others can recover them.
